text:
1. Why bearings fail and why vibration is monitored
Rolling element bearings support rotating shafts in motors, pumps, fans, compressors and gearboxes. Even a correctly selected bearing eventually fails by rolling contact fatigue, but most premature failures are caused by inadequate lubrication, contamination, misalignment, incorrect mounting, overloading or electrical current passing through the bearing. A localized defect such as a spall, pit or crack on the outer race, inner race or a rolling element produces a short mechanical impact every time a rolling element passes over it. These impacts excite structural resonances of the bearing housing at high frequency (typically 1 kHz to 10 kHz), which is why accelerometers mounted on the housing are the standard sensor for bearing condition monitoring.
Vibration monitoring detects bearing damage weeks or months before functional failure. The interval between the first detectable symptom (point P) and functional failure (point F) is called the P-F interval. Inspection and data-collection frequency must be shorter than the P-F interval, otherwise the defect can progress to failure between two measurements.
title: Vibration-Based Diagnosis of Rolling Element Bearings - Fundamentals

text:
2. Time-domain condition indicators
Root mean square (RMS) measures the overall energy of the vibration signal. RMS rises as damage grows, but it is insensitive to early, small localized defects because the impacts are short and carry little energy.
Kurtosis measures how impulsive (peaky) a signal is. A healthy bearing produces approximately Gaussian vibration with a kurtosis close to 3. Localized defects produce periodic impulses and raise kurtosis well above 3; values above about 4 to 5 indicate impulsive content and values above 8 to 10 indicate strong impacting. High kurtosis is therefore an early indicator of a localized race or rolling-element defect. Kurtosis can fall again at an advanced stage when damage spreads around the race and the signal becomes more random, so kurtosis must be trended together with RMS.
Crest factor is the ratio of peak amplitude to RMS. A sine wave has a crest factor of 1.41 and Gaussian noise typically 3 to 4. Crest factor values above about 5 to 6 indicate impacting. Like kurtosis, crest factor rises early and may fall in the final stage of degradation when RMS increases strongly.
Skewness describes asymmetry of the amplitude distribution. It is less widely used but can change when impacts occur preferentially in one direction, for example because of load-zone effects.
title: Vibration-Based Diagnosis of Rolling Element Bearings - Fundamentals

text:
3. Frequency-domain indicators and FFT band energy
The fast Fourier transform (FFT) converts a time window into a spectrum. Band energy features divide the spectrum into frequency bands and measure the share of energy in each band. Bearing defects typically increase energy in the high-frequency bands where housing resonances are excited, while unbalance and misalignment increase energy at 1x and 2x running speed. A rising share of energy above 2 kHz is a typical early sign of bearing damage or lubrication problems.
title: Vibration-Based Diagnosis of Rolling Element Bearings - Fundamentals

text:
4. Envelope analysis (demodulation)
Envelope analysis is the most reliable classical method to confirm a bearing defect. The signal is band-pass filtered around a resonance band excited by the impacts, the envelope is computed (for example with the Hilbert transform), and the spectrum of the envelope is calculated. Peaks in the envelope spectrum at a bearing defect frequency and its harmonics identify the damaged component: BPFO for the outer race, BPFI for the inner race, two times BSF for a rolling element, and FTF for the cage. Inner race defects usually show sidebands spaced at shaft speed around BPFI because the defect moves in and out of the load zone once per revolution. Outer race defects on a stationary outer ring usually show clean BPFO harmonics without shaft-speed sidebands.
Rolling element (ball) defects are the hardest to confirm with envelope analysis because the ball spins and the defect does not strike a race on every revolution. Published benchmark studies on the Case Western Reserve University dataset report that many ball-fault recordings do not show clear ball-spin frequency components.
title: Vibration-Based Diagnosis of Rolling Element Bearings - Fundamentals

text:
1. Kinematic defect frequency formulas
For a bearing with n rolling elements, ball diameter d, pitch diameter D, contact angle phi and shaft rotation frequency fr = rpm / 60 (rotating inner ring, stationary outer ring), the characteristic defect frequencies are:
- Fundamental train (cage) frequency: FTF = (fr / 2) x (1 - (d / D) cos phi)
- Ball pass frequency, outer race: BPFO = (n x fr / 2) x (1 - (d / D) cos phi)
- Ball pass frequency, inner race: BPFI = (n x fr / 2) x (1 + (d / D) cos phi)
- Ball spin frequency: BSF = (D / 2d) x fr x (1 - ((d / D) cos phi)^2)
These formulas assume pure rolling without slip. In real machines the observed frequencies differ by 1 to 2 percent because of slip, so frequency matching should use a tolerance band of a few percent. BPFO plus BPFI equals n times the shaft frequency, which is a useful sanity check.
title: Bearing Defect Frequencies and the CWRU Test Bearing

text:
2. The CWRU drive-end test bearing (SKF 6205-2RS JEM)
The Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing test rig uses a 2 hp induction motor, a torque transducer/encoder and a dynamometer. The drive-end bearing is a deep-groove ball bearing SKF 6205-2RS JEM with 9 balls, ball diameter 0.3126 inch (7.94 mm), pitch diameter 1.537 inch (39.04 mm) and a contact angle of zero.
Expressed as multiples of shaft speed, the drive-end defect frequencies are approximately: BPFI 5.415, BPFO 3.585, FTF 0.398 and BSF 2.357. At 1797 rpm (0 hp load, shaft frequency 29.95 Hz) this gives BPFI of about 162.2 Hz, BPFO of about 107.4 Hz and BSF of about 70.6 Hz. At 1730 rpm (3 hp load) BPFI is about 156.1 Hz and BPFO about 103.4 Hz.
title: Bearing Defect Frequencies and the CWRU Test Bearing

text:
3. CWRU seeded faults and operating conditions
Single-point faults were introduced with electro-discharge machining at diameters of 0.007, 0.014 and 0.021 inch (0.178, 0.356 and 0.533 mm) on the inner race, the rolling element and the outer race. Outer race faults were placed at the 3, 6 and 12 o'clock positions relative to the load zone; the 6 o'clock position is centred in the load zone and is the most commonly used. Each fault was recorded at motor loads of 0, 1, 2 and 3 hp with speeds of approximately 1797, 1772, 1750 and 1730 rpm.
Drive-end fault data are available at 12 kHz and 48 kHz sampling rates. The normal baseline recordings were sampled at 48 kHz, so they must be resampled to 12 kHz before being combined with 12 kHz fault data; otherwise a classifier can learn the sampling rate instead of the bearing condition.
title: Bearing Defect Frequencies and the CWRU Test Bearing

text:
4. Using defect frequencies in a diagnosis
A diagnosis is strongest when three independent indicators agree: (1) an elevated impulsiveness indicator such as kurtosis or crest factor, (2) envelope spectrum peaks at the matching defect frequency with harmonics, and (3) a data-driven classifier prediction with high confidence. When the classifier and the defect-frequency evidence disagree, the result should be treated as uncertain and confirmed by a qualified analyst before any maintenance action.
title: Bearing Defect Frequencies and the CWRU Test Bearing

text:
1. Vibration signature of an outer race fault
An outer race defect on a stationary outer ring is struck by every rolling element as it passes through the defect location. This produces a series of impacts at the ball pass frequency of the outer race (BPFO). Because the defect does not move relative to the load zone, the impact amplitude is nearly constant and the envelope spectrum shows a clean series of BPFO harmonics (1x, 2x, 3x BPFO) usually without shaft-speed sidebands. Time-domain kurtosis is typically high (often above 5) and crest factor is elevated at the early and middle stages of damage. A defect located in the load zone (6 o'clock position) produces the strongest signature; defects outside the load zone (3 or 12 o'clock) can be much weaker and may be missed by amplitude thresholds.
title: Outer Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
2. Typical root causes
Common root causes of outer race damage are: rolling contact fatigue at the end of the rated life; inadequate or degraded lubrication causing surface distress; hard particle contamination producing indentations that grow into spalls; a housing seat that is out of round or too tight (pinched outer ring), producing two load zones; static overload or impact during handling that creates brinell marks spaced at the ball pitch; and electrical current passage, which produces fluting (washboard pattern) on the outer race.
title: Outer Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
3. Recommended actions when an outer race fault is indicated
When the classifier and envelope spectrum indicate an outer race fault with high kurtosis, the following actions are recommended:
1. Verify the finding: repeat the measurement, confirm the BPFO peak and harmonics in the envelope spectrum and check that the shaft speed used for the calculation is correct.
2. Increase monitoring frequency (for example from monthly to weekly or daily) and trend RMS, kurtosis and the BPFO envelope amplitude.
3. Check lubrication: confirm the correct grease or oil, quantity and relubrication interval; take a lubricant sample if possible and look for metallic particles.
4. Inspect the housing fit and alignment at the next opportunity.
5. Plan bearing replacement at the next scheduled stop. Replace immediately if RMS rises rapidly, temperature increases, audible noise appears or envelope amplitude grows across consecutive measurements.
6. After removal, inspect the outer ring raceway, record the damage location relative to the load zone and classify the failure mode (for example according to ISO 15243) to address the root cause.
title: Outer Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
4. Severity guidance
Small isolated spalls (early stage) often show high kurtosis with only modest RMS increase. As the spall grows, RMS increases and kurtosis may decrease because the impacts merge. A combination of rising RMS, rising broadband noise floor and falling kurtosis indicates advanced damage and a short remaining life. The decision to run to the next stop or to stop immediately must be taken by the responsible maintenance engineer.
title: Outer Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
1. Vibration signature of an inner race fault
On a machine with a rotating shaft the inner ring rotates with the shaft, so an inner race defect passes through the load zone once per shaft revolution. The rolling elements strike the defect at the ball pass frequency of the inner race (BPFI), and the impact strength is modulated by the load distribution. As a result, the envelope spectrum shows peaks at BPFI and its harmonics surrounded by sidebands spaced at the shaft rotation frequency (1x rpm). The presence of 1x sidebands around BPFI is a key feature that distinguishes inner race faults from outer race faults. Kurtosis is elevated, and the time waveform often shows impacts whose amplitude varies once per revolution.
title: Inner Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
2. Typical root causes
Common causes of inner race damage include: excessive interference fit on the shaft that reduces internal clearance and increases contact stress; insufficient or degraded lubrication; contamination; misalignment that loads the raceway edge; overloading; rolling contact fatigue; and mounting damage such as hammer blows transmitted through the rolling elements, which leave indentations (false or true brinelling) on the inner race.
title: Inner Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
3. Recommended actions when an inner race fault is indicated
1. Confirm the diagnosis: check the envelope spectrum for BPFI harmonics with 1x rpm sidebands and verify the running speed.
2. Increase the monitoring interval frequency and trend kurtosis, RMS and BPFI amplitude; inner race faults often progress faster than outer race faults because the defect passes through the load zone every revolution.
3. Check lubrication condition and relubrication interval.
4. Check shaft fit, alignment and operating load; look for signs of overheating such as discoloration or increased bearing temperature.
5. Schedule replacement at the earliest planned stop; stop immediately if temperature, noise or vibration rises quickly.
6. After removal, inspect the inner ring raceway and shaft seat, document the damage pattern and identify the root cause before reinstalling a new bearing, using correct mounting tools (induction heater or press, never direct hammer blows on the rings).
title: Inner Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
4. Severity guidance
Because the defect travels through the load zone, inner race spalls can grow quickly once started. An increasing BPFI envelope amplitude over successive measurements, rising temperature and a growing number of harmonics are signs that the remaining life is short.
title: Inner Race Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
1. Vibration signature of a ball (rolling element) fault
A defect on a rolling element strikes the inner and outer race alternately as the ball spins, so the characteristic frequency is twice the ball spin frequency (2 x BSF), often with sidebands at the cage frequency (FTF) because the defective ball moves in and out of the load zone with the cage. Ball defects frequently produce weaker and less regular signatures than race defects: the ball can change its spin axis, so the defect does not hit the races on every rotation. As a consequence, envelope spectra of ball faults are often inconclusive, and diagnosis relies more on overall impulsiveness indicators (kurtosis, crest factor), high-frequency band energy and data-driven classifiers.
title: Rolling Element (Ball) Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
2. Typical root causes
Ball defects are caused by contamination (hard particles rolled into the ball surface), inadequate lubrication, material inclusions, electrical erosion, or damage during handling and mounting. A single damaged ball can quickly damage the raceways, so a ball defect should be treated as a precursor to race damage.
title: Rolling Element (Ball) Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
3. Recommended actions when a ball fault is indicated
1. Because envelope confirmation is often weak for ball faults, confirm the prediction by trending kurtosis, crest factor and high-frequency energy over several measurements rather than relying on a single reading.
2. Check the lubricant for contamination and metal particles; check seals and shields for damage.
3. Increase the measurement frequency and look for the appearance of BPFO or BPFI components, which indicate that the damage has spread to the raceways.
4. Plan bearing replacement at the next convenient stop. A bearing with a rolling-element defect cannot be repaired in the field.
5. After removal, inspect all rolling elements and both raceways and document the failure mode.
title: Rolling Element (Ball) Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
4. Diagnostic caution
When a classifier predicts a ball fault but no characteristic frequency is visible in the envelope spectrum, the result should be presented as uncertain and confirmed by an experienced analyst. Conversely, when the envelope spectrum shows strong inner race or outer race harmonics, these should be investigated even if the classifier predicts a ball fault.
title: Rolling Element (Ball) Faults - Signatures, Causes and Inspection Actions

text:
1. Role of lubrication
The lubricant separates the rolling elements from the raceways with a thin film, reduces friction and wear, protects against corrosion and, for oil, removes heat. Inadequate lubrication is one of the most frequent causes of premature bearing failure. Symptoms include rising bearing temperature, a rising high-frequency noise floor in the vibration spectrum, increased high-frequency band energy and, in later stages, surface distress (glazing, micro-spalling) on the raceways.
title: Bearing Lubrication, Contamination Control and Related Failure Modes

text:
2. Relubrication practice
Relubrication intervals depend on bearing type, size, speed, temperature and environment and should be taken from the bearing or machine manufacturer's recommendations. Over-greasing is also harmful: too much grease causes churning, high temperature and seal damage. Use the specified grease type and do not mix incompatible greases. Clean the grease fitting before relubrication to avoid introducing dirt. Record each relubrication in the maintenance log so that vibration changes can be correlated with lubrication events.
title: Bearing Lubrication, Contamination Control and Related Failure Modes

text:
3. Contamination
Solid contaminants (dust, sand, metal particles from wear or machining) are rolled into the raceways and create dents. Stress concentrations at dent edges start fatigue cracks that grow into spalls. Liquid contaminants such as water reduce lubricant film strength and cause corrosion. Contamination control measures include effective seals and shields, clean handling during mounting, filtered oil systems and closing grease containers.
title: Bearing Lubrication, Contamination Control and Related Failure Modes

text:
4. Lubricant analysis
Oil or grease samples can be analysed for wear metal particles (iron, chromium for bearing steel), water content and oxidation. A rising concentration of bearing-steel particles combined with increasing vibration kurtosis or envelope amplitude supports a diagnosis of active bearing damage.
title: Bearing Lubrication, Contamination Control and Related Failure Modes

text:
5. Interpreting vibration after relubrication
If high-frequency vibration and the noise floor fall significantly after relubrication and stay low, the problem was a lubrication deficiency rather than a localized defect. If impacting at a defect frequency persists or returns within days, a localized defect is present and replacement should be planned.
title: Bearing Lubrication, Contamination Control and Related Failure Modes

text:
1. Safety before any work
Before inspecting or replacing a bearing, the machine must be stopped and isolated using the site lockout/tagout (LOTO) procedure: switch off, isolate all energy sources (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, stored mechanical energy), lock and tag the isolation points and verify zero energy by attempting a start. Allow hot bearings and housings to cool. Use the required personal protective equipment such as gloves and safety glasses.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
2. Pre-removal inspection and documentation
Record the machine identifier, running hours, recent vibration readings, temperature trend and lubrication history. Check for loose foundation bolts, coupling wear and misalignment, because these can produce vibration that resembles bearing problems. Photograph the assembly before dismounting and mark the orientation of the bearing relative to the load zone.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
3. Dismounting
Use a mechanical or hydraulic puller, or hydraulic (oil injection) methods for large bearings. Apply the dismounting force to the ring with the interference fit. Do not strike the bearing rings or rolling elements directly with a hammer. Keep the removed bearing for failure analysis: do not clean away evidence before inspection.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
4. Failure analysis of the removed bearing
Inspect the raceways, rolling elements, cage and seals. Note the location and shape of any damage and the load-zone pattern (the running track). Classify the damage according to ISO 15243 failure mode categories: fatigue (subsurface or surface-initiated), wear (abrasive or adhesive), corrosion (moisture, fretting or false brinelling), electrical erosion (excessive current, current leakage/fluting), plastic deformation (overload or indentation from debris) and fracture and cracking. Identifying the failure mode is necessary to remove the root cause; otherwise the new bearing is likely to fail the same way.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
5. Mounting the new bearing
Check shaft and housing seats for size, roundness and damage. Mount with correct tools: an induction heater for interference fits on the shaft or a mounting sleeve and press, never hammer blows through the rolling elements. Use the correct lubricant and quantity. After mounting, check that the shaft rotates freely, re-align the coupling, and record baseline vibration (RMS, kurtosis, envelope spectrum) after a run-in period so that future measurements can be compared against it.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
6. Return to service
Remove locks and tags only after all tools are cleared and personnel are informed. Measure vibration and temperature during the first hours of operation and update the maintenance log with the work order number, findings and the root cause.
title: Bearing Inspection, Dismounting and Replacement Procedure

text:
1. Baselines and trending
An effective condition monitoring programme records a baseline for each machine after commissioning or after a bearing replacement, then measures at a fixed interval under comparable operating conditions (speed and load). Decisions are based on trends: a steady increase in RMS, kurtosis, high-frequency band energy or envelope amplitude at a defect frequency is more informative than any single absolute reading. Because vibration amplitude depends on speed and load, readings taken at different loads must be compared with care; data-driven models should be validated on load conditions not seen during training.
title: Condition Monitoring Programme, Alarm Levels and Decision Making

text:
2. Alarm levels
Typical programmes use two alarm levels. An alert (warning) level is often set at about two to three times the baseline value of an indicator and triggers increased monitoring and a planned inspection. A danger level, often set at about four to six times baseline or at a machine-specific limit, triggers a recommendation to stop or replace at the earliest opportunity. For overall velocity vibration of the machine, the ISO 10816 / ISO 20816 series defines evaluation zones (A: newly commissioned, B: acceptable for long-term operation, C: unsatisfactory for long-term operation, D: severe enough to cause damage), with zone limits that depend on machine group, size and support type; the applicable part of the standard should be consulted for exact values.
title: Condition Monitoring Programme, Alarm Levels and Decision Making

text:
3. Stages of bearing degradation
Bearing degradation is commonly described in four stages. Stage 1: ultrasonic and high-frequency acoustic emission only; standard vibration is normal. Stage 2: small defects excite bearing component natural frequencies; high-frequency energy and kurtosis increase. Stage 3: defect frequencies and harmonics appear clearly in the spectrum and envelope spectrum, often with sidebands; the bearing should be scheduled for replacement. Stage 4: broadband noise floor rises, discrete defect frequencies may disappear into random vibration, RMS and temperature increase; failure is near.
title: Condition Monitoring Programme, Alarm Levels and Decision Making

text:
4. Decision support and human review
Automated diagnostic tools, including machine-learning classifiers and AI assistants, should be used as decision support. Their output must be reviewed by a qualified person before maintenance decisions are made, particularly when the tool reports low confidence, when the indicators disagree, or when the recommended action involves stopping a critical machine. Every recommendation should be traceable to the measured data and to the procedure or manual that supports it.
title: Condition Monitoring Programme, Alarm Levels and Decision Making

text:
1. Why non-bearing faults matter for bearing diagnosis
Many vibration problems that are reported as "bearing noise" are caused by other machine faults. These faults also shorten bearing life because they increase bearing load. Before replacing a bearing, the analyst should rule out unbalance, misalignment and mechanical looseness.
title: Non-Bearing Vibration Sources - Unbalance, Misalignment and Looseness

text:
2. Unbalance
Unbalance produces a dominant sinusoidal component at 1x running speed in the radial direction, with low kurtosis (close to 3 or below) and a crest factor close to that of a sine wave. Amplitude increases with the square of speed. Correction is by field balancing; replacing the bearing does not fix unbalance.
title: Non-Bearing Vibration Sources - Unbalance, Misalignment and Looseness

text:
3. Misalignment
Shaft misalignment between coupled machines produces high 1x and 2x running-speed components, often with high axial vibration and a phase difference of about 180 degrees across the coupling. Misalignment increases bearing loads and can cause premature raceway wear along one edge. Correction is by laser or dial-indicator alignment.
title: Non-Bearing Vibration Sources - Unbalance, Misalignment and Looseness

text:
4. Mechanical looseness
Looseness of bearing housings, foundation bolts or a bearing that turns on its shaft produces many harmonics of running speed (1x, 2x, 3x ... often up to 10x) and sometimes half-order components. Looseness of a bearing in its housing can also produce random impacting that raises kurtosis, so it can be confused with a bearing defect. Check bolt torque and fits before concluding that the bearing itself is damaged.
title: Non-Bearing Vibration Sources - Unbalance, Misalignment and Looseness

text:
5. Electrical sources in motors
Electrically induced vibration at twice line frequency (100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply, 120 Hz on a 60 Hz supply) disappears immediately when power is switched off, whereas mechanical vibration decays with speed. Shaft currents from variable frequency drives can cause electrical erosion (fluting) of bearing raceways; insulated bearings or shaft grounding are used as countermeasures.
title: Non-Bearing Vibration Sources - Unbalance, Misalignment and Looseness

text:
1. How a rolling bearing carries load
A rolling bearing transfers the shaft load through very small contact areas between the rolling elements and the raceways. Because the contact area is tiny, the contact pressure is very high, typically between 1 and 4 GPa in a loaded ball bearing. This pressure is called Hertzian contact stress. The highest shear stress does not occur on the surface but a short distance below it, usually a few tenths of a millimetre under the raceway. Every time a ball rolls over a point on the raceway, that point is loaded and unloaded once, so a bearing running at 1800 rpm applies millions of stress cycles to its raceways every day.
Only part of the bearing carries load at any moment. Under a radial load the rolling elements at the bottom of a horizontal shaft carry most of the force; this region is called the load zone. A defect inside the load zone is hit hard, while the same defect outside the load zone is hit gently or not at all. The load zone is the key to understanding why the vibration of each fault type looks different.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
2. Rolling contact fatigue: the natural way a bearing fails
Even a perfectly installed and lubricated bearing eventually fails by rolling contact fatigue. The repeated stress cycles below the surface start a microscopic crack, often at a small non-metallic inclusion in the steel. The crack grows slowly parallel to the surface and then turns up towards the raceway. When it reaches the surface, a small flake of material breaks out and leaves a cavity called a spall or pit. This process is called spalling or flaking, and ISO 15243 classifies it as subsurface-initiated fatigue.
The rated life of a bearing (L10 life) is the number of revolutions that 90 percent of a group of identical bearings will complete before the first sign of fatigue spalling. Real bearings rarely reach this natural fatigue limit, because most failures are premature and are caused by the operating conditions.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
3. Causes of premature bearing damage
Surface-initiated fatigue happens when the lubricant film is too thin to separate the surfaces, so the asperities of the ball and the raceway touch. Insufficient lubricant, the wrong viscosity, degraded grease, high temperature or too long a relubrication interval all thin the film and start micro-pitting on the surface.
Contamination is one of the most common causes of early failure. Hard particles such as sand, metal chips or grinding dust are over-rolled and press dents into the raceways. Each dent has raised edges that concentrate stress, so a spall often starts just behind a dent. Water or moisture causes corrosion pits that act in the same way.
Incorrect mounting damages a bearing before it ever runs. Hammer blows transmitted through the rolling elements, or forcing the bearing onto the shaft through the wrong ring, leave indentations at the ball spacing called true brinelling. Vibration while the machine is stopped can wear similar marks called false brinelling.
Misalignment and overload concentrate the load on one edge of the raceway or on fewer rolling elements, which raises the contact stress and shortens fatigue life sharply. An interference fit that is too tight removes internal clearance and has the same effect.
Electric current passing through the bearing, for example from a variable frequency drive without shaft grounding, causes tiny arcs across the lubricant film. These arcs melt small craters and eventually produce a washboard pattern on the raceway called fluting.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
4. How a defect produces vibration
When a rolling element passes over a spall, it drops into the cavity and strikes the far edge. Each strike is a short mechanical impact lasting well under a millisecond. The impact excites the natural resonances of the bearing, the housing and the sensor mount, which typically lie between 1 kHz and 10 kHz, so each impact appears in the vibration signal as a short burst of ringing that decays quickly.
Because the shaft turns at a constant speed and the balls are evenly spaced, the impacts repeat at a regular rate that depends on where the defect is. This repetition rate is the bearing defect frequency: BPFO for the outer race, BPFI for the inner race and BSF for a rolling element. The defect frequencies themselves are low, usually between 50 Hz and 300 Hz, but the energy of the impacts sits at the high resonance frequencies.
Envelope analysis recovers the hidden repetition rate. The signal is band-pass filtered around the resonance, the envelope (the outline of the bursts) is calculated with the Hilbert transform, and a spectrum of the envelope is taken. Peaks at the defect frequency and its harmonics in the envelope spectrum show that the bursts repeat at that rate, which identifies the faulty component.
Statistical indicators react to the impacts as well. Sharp bursts on a quiet background raise the kurtosis well above the value of 3 that a healthy, Gaussian-like signal shows, and they raise the crest factor, which is the ratio of peak to RMS. As damage spreads, the impacts merge, RMS rises and kurtosis can fall again, so a falling kurtosis is not always a sign of improvement.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
5. Why an outer race fault looks the way it does
The outer ring is normally stationary in the housing, so an outer race defect stays at the same position. If the defect lies in the load zone, every rolling element that passes over it strikes it with about the same force. The result is a train of evenly spaced impacts of nearly constant amplitude at BPFO. The envelope spectrum shows clear peaks at BPFO and its harmonics without strong sidebands, which is the classic and easiest bearing fault to detect. In the CWRU data the outer race faults were placed at the 6 o'clock position, which is centred in the load zone, so they give strong BPFO lines.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
6. Why an inner race fault looks the way it does
The inner ring rotates with the shaft, so an inner race defect travels around with it. Once per shaft revolution the defect passes through the load zone, where the impacts are strong, and then moves out of it, where they become weak. The impact amplitude is therefore modulated at the shaft rotation frequency. In the envelope spectrum this produces peaks at BPFI with sidebands spaced at 1x shaft speed on each side. The impacts are also transmitted to the sensor through more interfaces, the rolling elements and the outer ring, so they arrive weaker than outer race impacts and are often harder to detect at an early stage. Inner race damage tends to progress quickly because the defect is loaded on every revolution.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
7. Why a ball fault looks the way it does
A defect on a rolling element spins with the ball and strikes the inner race and the outer race alternately. It therefore produces impacts at twice the ball spin frequency (2 x BSF). The ball also travels around the bearing with the cage, moving in and out of the load zone, so the impacts are modulated at the cage frequency (FTF) and the envelope spectrum shows sidebands at FTF. A ball can also roll so that the defect does not touch the races on every turn, which makes the impacts irregular. For these reasons ball faults are the hardest bearing faults to detect with envelope analysis.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
8. Stages of bearing degradation
Bearing failure develops in stages. In stage 1 the first subsurface damage creates only ultrasonic emission and is not visible in normal vibration spectra. In stage 2 small defects begin to ring the bearing resonances, so high-frequency energy, kurtosis and envelope readings rise. In stage 3 the defect frequencies and their harmonics appear clearly in the envelope and velocity spectra, and sidebands grow as the damage spreads. In stage 4 the discrete frequencies are replaced by a raised broadband noise floor, RMS and temperature rise quickly, and the bearing is close to failure. Trending these indicators over successive measurements shows how fast a bearing is moving through the stages and how much time is left to plan a replacement.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
9. Seeded faults in test rigs compared with real faults
Laboratory datasets such as CWRU use seeded faults made by electro-discharge machining, which cuts a clean round pit of a known diameter into the raceway or ball. A seeded pit gives sharp, repeatable impacts, which makes it easier to classify than natural fatigue damage. Natural spalls have irregular edges, grow over time and are usually accompanied by wear, contamination and lubrication problems, so real signals are noisier. A model trained only on seeded faults should therefore be checked on new data before it is trusted on a different machine.
title: How Bearing Faults Occur - Damage Mechanisms and Why Each Fault Vibrates Differently

text:
1. What the CWRU dataset is
The Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) Bearing Data Center provides the most widely used public benchmark for bearing fault diagnosis. The test rig consists of a 2 hp Reliance Electric induction motor, a torque transducer and encoder, and a dynamometer that applies the load. Accelerometers mounted on the motor housing near the drive-end bearing and the fan-end bearing record the vibration, and the motor speed is recorded with each file.
Single-point faults were seeded into the drive-end bearing (SKF 6205-2RS JEM) with electro-discharge machining. The fault diameters used by IntelliMaintain are 0.007, 0.014 and 0.021 inch on the inner race, on a rolling element (ball) and on the outer race at the 6 o'clock position. Every condition was recorded at motor loads of 0, 1, 2 and 3 hp, which correspond to shaft speeds of about 1797, 1772, 1750 and 1730 rpm.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
2. The data IntelliMaintain is trained on
IntelliMaintain uses the standard 10-class benchmark from the 12 kHz drive-end experiments: Normal, B_007, B_014, B_021, IR_007, IR_014, IR_021, OR_007, OR_014 and OR_021. The letters give the fault location (B for ball, IR for inner race, OR for outer race) and the number gives the fault diameter in thousandths of an inch. With 10 classes at 4 loads, the training set contains 40 recordings.
The CWRU normal baseline files were recorded at 48 kHz while the fault files were recorded at 12 kHz. IntelliMaintain anti-alias filters and decimates the normal files by 4 so that every class shares the same 12 kHz time base; without this step a classifier can learn the sampling rate instead of the bearing condition.
Each recording is cut into windows of 2048 samples (about 0.17 seconds at 12 kHz) with 50 percent overlap, which gives 4643 windows from the 40 recordings. Every window becomes one training example with the label of its recording.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

Most fault classes raise RMS, kurtosis or crest factor because the rolling elements strike the defect. The relation to defect size is not simple: IR_014 and OR_021 have very high kurtosis, while OR_014 and B_007 have kurtosis close to 3. A single indicator therefore cannot separate all ten classes, which is why IntelliMaintain uses 29 features with a machine-learning model and adds the physics check.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
4. How IntelliMaintain compares a new signal with CWRU
For every uploaded signal, IntelliMaintain computes the same 29 features for each window and averages them. It then measures the distance between this average and the average feature vector of each of the 40 CWRU recordings, after standardising every feature. The three closest recordings are reported as the most similar CWRU cases with a similarity between 0 and 1. If the closest recordings share the predicted fault type, the prediction is supported by case-based evidence; if they disagree, the result should be treated with caution.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
5. How well the models perform on CWRU
With a random 80/20 split of the windows, the RandomForest reaches an accuracy of 1.0000. A random split is optimistic, because overlapping windows from the same recording can appear in both the training and the test set. In the cross-load test the models are trained on loads 0 to 2 hp and tested on the unseen 3 hp load, and the RandomForest still reaches an accuracy of 1.0000. In leave-one-load-out testing the mean accuracy is 0.9995.
The hardest test is cross-severity generalisation: the models are trained on 0.007 and 0.014 inch faults and tested on unseen 0.021 inch faults. Here the accuracy drops to 0.4268 for the RandomForest and 0.4359 for the spectrogram CNN, because a new defect size changes the signal more than a new load does. This is the honest limit of models trained only on CWRU.
Under added noise on the cross-load test, the RandomForest accuracy falls from 1.0000 on clean data to 0.4058 at 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio. The spectrogram CNN trained with noise augmentation keeps 0.9618 at 5 dB, and a RandomForest trained with the same augmentation reaches 0.9652, so most of the robustness comes from the augmentation.
Isotonic calibration reduced the expected calibration error of the RandomForest from 0.1203 to 0.0163 on the unseen 3 hp load, so its confidence values can be read as probabilities.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
6. What the physics check achieves on CWRU
The envelope-spectrum physics check, used on its own without machine learning, identifies the fault type of 0.600 of the CWRU recordings. It identifies 1.000 of the inner race and normal recordings and 0.667 of the outer race recordings, but none of the ball faults, because ball defects produce weak and irregular impacts at twice the ball spin frequency. For this reason the physics check is used to confirm or question the classifier, not to replace it.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
7. Limits of a model trained on CWRU
CWRU contains seeded faults from a single motor, a single bearing type and steady speeds between 1730 and 1797 rpm. A model trained only on CWRU should not be trusted blindly on a different machine, bearing, speed range or sensor position. Before use on a new machine, the model should be checked with labelled data from that machine, and low-confidence or conflicting results should always be verified by a vibration analyst.
title: The CWRU Bearing Dataset and How IntelliMaintain Learns From It

text:
0. What a bearing is
A bearing is a machine element that supports a rotating shaft and lets it turn with very little friction. A rolling-element bearing, also called a rolling bearing or ball bearing, has an inner ring fixed on the shaft, an outer ring fixed in the housing, rolling elements such as balls or rollers between the two rings, and a cage that keeps the rolling elements evenly spaced. Bearings are used in almost every rotating machine, including electric motors, pumps, fans, compressors and gearboxes, and a bearing failure is one of the most common reasons for an unplanned machine stop.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
1. What IntelliMaintain does
IntelliMaintain is an AI copilot for bearing maintenance. It diagnoses the condition of a rolling-element bearing from a vibration signal, explains how the fault develops, and recommends maintenance actions with a citation for every statement. Its output is advisory: a qualified engineer reviews every answer and accepts, rejects or edits it before any action is taken.
A diagnosis runs in four steps. First, a machine-learning classifier predicts the bearing condition from the vibration signal. Second, a physics check calculates the bearing defect frequencies from the shaft speed and looks for them in the envelope spectrum. Third, a retrieval system searches the maintenance documents, and optionally the web, for passages about the fault. Fourth, a language model or the offline generator writes the answer using only that evidence, and every sentence is checked against the source it cites.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
2. What the citations mean
A citation in square brackets shows where each statement comes from. [ML] means the statement comes from the machine-learning classifier. [PHYS] means it comes from the physics check of the defect frequencies. A number such as [2] refers to evidence passage 2 in the evidence list, which comes from a maintenance manual, guideline or maintenance log. A citation such as [W1] refers to web evidence passage 1, which comes from an online source and is shown with its link. Sentences that cannot be matched to the source they cite are removed automatically.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
3. What the confidence and anomaly score mean
The confidence is the calibrated probability of the predicted class, averaged over all 2048-sample windows of the signal. A confidence of 0.95 means that, on test data, predictions with this confidence were correct about 95 percent of the time. Below 0.60 the result is flagged as low confidence and should be verified by an analyst.
The anomaly score comes from an Isolation Forest trained on the CWRU recordings. It ranges from 0, which means the signal looks like the data the model was trained on, to 1, which means the signal is unusual. A high anomaly score warns that the signal may come from a machine or condition the model has never seen, even if the confidence is high.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
4. What the physics cross-check means
The physics check calculates the defect frequencies BPFO, BPFI and BSF from the bearing geometry and the shaft speed, then measures how strongly each frequency and its harmonics stand out in the envelope spectrum. A ratio above 5 means the frequency is present. If the physics check points to the same fault as the classifier, the result is consistent. If it points to a different fault, the result is a conflict and the answer asks for analyst verification instead of giving a fault type. If no frequency stands out, the result is inconclusive, which is common for normal bearings and for ball faults.
The shaft speed entered in the app directly changes the defect frequencies, so a wrong speed can make the physics check miss a real fault. The sampling rate must match the recording, because the signal is resampled to 12 kHz before analysis.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
5. Which files can be uploaded
The app accepts vibration recordings as CSV, TXT, MAT or NPY files. A CSV file can contain a single column of acceleration values or several columns; the app uses the column with the vibration signal. The recording must contain at least 2048 samples at 12 kHz, and longer recordings of several seconds give more reliable results because more windows are averaged. The app also offers demo samples taken from the CWRU dataset.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
6. What "insufficient evidence" means
Insufficient evidence means that neither the classifier nor the documents give enough information to answer the question reliably. IntelliMaintain does not guess in this case. The question can be rephrased, a vibration recording can be uploaded, or online search can be enabled so that web sources are searched as well.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
7. Which models are used
The default classifier is a RandomForest trained on 29 features per window: 10 time-domain statistics such as RMS, kurtosis and crest factor, 3 spectral shape features and 16 frequency-band energies. Its probabilities are calibrated with isotonic regression. The second classifier is a convolutional neural network that classifies a 64 by 64 spectrogram image of each window. Both classify 10 CWRU classes, which are combined into four fault types: Normal, Inner race, Outer race and Ball.
The knowledge retrieval combines dense embedding search with BM25 keyword search and merges both rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. The language model is Google Gemini, used through its API with a low temperature. When no API key is configured, when the quota is used up or when the answer fails verification, an offline extractive generator builds the answer from the evidence instead, so the app always works.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
8. Whether the machine can keep running
The decision to keep a machine running depends on the severity and the trend, not on a single measurement. A normal result means routine monitoring can continue. A fault in an early stage usually allows the machine to run with more frequent monitoring until a planned stop, while a rapid rise in vibration, temperature or noise means the machine should be stopped. The final decision belongs to the responsible engineer and must follow the site's safety rules, including lockout and tagout before any work on the machine.
title: IntelliMaintain - Frequently Asked Questions About the System and Its Results

text:
9. Differences between the fault types in plain words
An outer race fault is damage on the stationary outer ring; it gives regular impacts of equal strength at BPFO and is usually the easiest fault to detect. An inner race fault is damage on the rotating inner ring; it gives impacts at BPFI whose strength rises and falls once per revolution, which adds sidebands at shaft speed. A ball fault is damage on a rolling element; it gives weaker, irregular impacts at twice the ball spin frequency with sidebands at the cage frequency and is the hardest to detect. A normal bearing shows no repeating impacts, low RMS and a kurtosis close to 3.

text:
1 Introduction Rotating machinery is widely used in many industrial ﬁelds. Fault diagnosis in rotating machinery is important for system maintenance and process automation. In practice, faulty bearings contribute to most of the failures in rotating machinery [1, 2, 3, 4]. It is reported that about 40% to 90% of failures are related to rolling element bearing failures from large to small machines [5]. Particularly, either inner-race or outer-race ﬂaws dominate most bearing failures. Periodic sharp impulses characterize these faults, and the characteristic frequencies can be theoretically computed. Nevertheless those impulses are of low power and usually buried by noises. These signals are also usually modulated by some high-frequency harmonic components and resulted in a series of harmonics of characteristic frequencies [6].
In order to realized fault diagnosis of bearing, some features of vibration signals are extracted through time-domain methods, frequency-domain methods, and time-frequency methods [2]. Time-domain methods are directly based on the time waveform, e.g. peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, variance, skewness, kurtosis, correlation dimension and fractal dimension.
Frequencydomain methods are based on the transformed signal in frequency domain, i.e. Fourier spectrum, cepstrum analysis, envelope spectrum. Wavelet analysis, short time Fourier transform, Wigner-Ville distribution and Hilbert-Huang transform are the time-frequency methods [?, 7, 8, 9, 10], which investigate waveform signals in both time and frequency domain. When used to analyse noisy bearing vibration signals, most of those methods may produce unsatisfactory results and may not give useful information about the characteristic frequencies in order to identify the faults.
Spectral kurtosis was developed to identify the characteristic frequencies of bearings, where a ﬁlter was designed to get the signal with the maximum kurtosis in spectrum and then the envelope analysis was usually applied to show the characteristic frequencies [11, 12, 13]. The wavelet techniques were widely used to decompose the vibration signals in order to ﬁnd the most useful ﬁlter for fault diagnosis [14, 15, 16, 17].
The conventional band-pass ﬁlters were also applied whose parameters were optimized through genetic algorithms or adaptive algorithms [18, 19]. Those methods are relatively complex which 2

Indeed spectral kurtosis based methods are to ﬁnd the resonant frequency band of vibration signals which contains a train of high-energy harmonics of characteristic frequency, and then transform the resonant frequency band to a low frequency band through envelope analysis. It is suggested that the characteristic frequency could be identiﬁed by ﬁnding harmonics with high energies in spectra. Reference [6] also pointed out that the impulses of bearing faults could be detected when a series of harmonics of the characteristic frequency are identiﬁed in the spectra.
This paper proposes a simple method to detect the faults of bearings by searching the harmonics in spectra. As discussed before, the impulses generated by bearing faults are usually modulated, and harmonics of the bearing characteristic frequency exist in the spectrum of vibration signals. Hence we simply search the local peaks in the spectrum of vibration signals. Then the local peaks related to harmonics of certain frequency is projected onto a predeﬁned frequency grid, such that the so-called structure information of the spectrum (SIOS) of the spectrum is constructed. The SIOS includes two deﬁned indexes, which provide the information about the number and the power of harmonics of certain frequency. The dominant and signiﬁcant components in the SIOS are just corresponding to the characteristic frequency of bearings and therefore the bearing faults can be diagnosed.

• inner-race fault: the dominant component in SIOS is BPFI,
• outer-race fault: the dominant component in SIOS is BPFO, and
• ball fault: the BFP, 2×BSF, and at least one harmonic of FTF are significant in SIOS; or 2× BSF is dominant in SIOS.

Although noises and other random impulses may introduce some local peaks unrelated to the faults, the signiﬁcant components in the SIOS can still be clearly recognized and related to the characteristic frequencies of bearings.

As illustrated in the benchmark study of bearings, the proposed method could provide more information about the harmonics of impulses than the envelope analysis and better diagnosis results can be achieved.

Deep Learning Algorithms for Rotating Machinery Intelligent Diagnosis: An Open Source Benchmark Study Zhibin Zhaoa, Tianfu Lia, Jingyao Wua, Chuang Suna, Shibin Wanga, Ruqiang Yana,∗, Xuefeng Chena aSchool of Mechanical Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, China Abstract Rotating machinery intelligent diagnosis based on deep learning (DL) has gone through tremendous progress, which can help reduce costly breakdowns.
However, diﬀerent datasets and hyper-parameters are recommended to be used, and few open source codes are publicly available, resulting in unfair comparisons and ineﬀective improvement.
To address these issues, we perform a comprehensive evaluation of four models, including multi-layer perception (MLP), autoencoder (AE), convolutional neural network (CNN), and recurrent neural network (RNN), with seven datasets to provide a benchmark study.
We ﬁrst gather nine publicly available datasets and give a comprehensive benchmark study of DL-based models with two data split strategies, ﬁve input formats, three normalization methods, and four augmentation methods.
Second, we integrate the whole evaluation codes into a code library and release it to the public for better comparisons.
Third, we use speciﬁc-designed cases to point out the existing issues, including class imbalance, generalization ability, interpretability, few-shot learning, and model selection. Finally, we release a uniﬁed code framework for comparing and testing models fairly and quickly, emphasize the importance of open source codes, provide the baseline accuracy (a lower bound), and discuss existing issues in this ﬁeld. The code library is available at: https://github.com/ZhaoZhibin/ DL-based-Intelligent-Diagnosis-Benchmark.
Keywords: Deep learning, machinery intelligent diagnosis, open source codes, benchmark study
1. Introduction Rotating machinery, as key mechanical equipment in the modern industry, is chronically running in a complex environment with elevated temperature, fatigue, and heavy load.
Generated faults might cause severe accidents, resulting in enormous economic loss and casualties.
Intelligent diagnosis, as a key ingredient of prognostics health management (PHM), which is one of the most essential systems in a wide range of rotating machinery, such as helicopter, aero-engine, wind turbine, and high-speed train, is designed to detect faults eﬀectively.
Traditional intelligent diagnosis methods mainly consist of feature extraction using signal processing methods [1, 2] and fault classiﬁcation [3] using machine learning approaches, which have made considerable progress.
However, facing with heterogeneous massive data, feature extraction methods and mapping abilities from signals to conditions that are designed and chosen by experts, to a great extent depending on prior knowledge, are time-consuming and empirical.
Thus, how to perform diagnosis more precisely and eﬃciently is still a challenging problem.

Due to its strong representation learning ability, DL is well-suited to data analysis and classiﬁcation.
Therefore, in the ﬁeld of intelligent diagnosis, many researchers have applied DL-based techniques, such as multi-layer perception (MLP), auto-encoder (AE), convolutional neural network (CNN), DBN, and recurrent neural network (RNN) to boost the performance.
However, diﬀerent researchers often recommended to use diﬀerent inputs (such as time domain input, frequency domain input, time-frequency domain input, etc.) and set diﬀerent hyper-parameters (such as the learning rate, the batch size, the network architecture, etc.).
Unfortunately, a few authors made their codes available for comparisons, resulting in unfair comparisons and ineﬀective improvement.
To address this problem, it is crucial to evaluate and compare diﬀerent DLbased intelligent diagnosis algorithms to provide the benchmark study and open souce codes, thereby helping further studies to propose more persuasive and appropriate algorithms.
For comprehensive performance comparisons, it is necessary to collect diﬀerent datasets in a library and evaluate the performance of algorithms for diﬀerent datasets on a uniﬁed platform. In addition, one common issue in intelligent diagnosis is data split, and researchers often use the random split strategy. This strategy is dangerous since if the preparation process exists any overlap, the evaluation of classiﬁcation algorithms will have test leakage [14]. As for industrial data, they are rarely random and are always sequential (they might contain trends in the time domain), and it is more appropriate to split data according to time sequences (we simply call it order split). Conversely, if we randomly split the data, it might be possible for diagnosis algorithms to record the future patterns, which might cause another pitfall with test leakage.
To address these problems, in this paper, we collect nine publicly available datasets and discuss whether it is suitable for intelligent diagnosis.
After that, we evaluate DL-based intelligent diagnosis algorithms from diﬀerent perspectives including the data preparation for all datasets and the whole evaluation framework with diﬀerent input formats, normalization methods, data split ways, augmentation methods, and DL-based models.
Based on the benchmark study, we highlight some evaluation results which are very important for comparing or testing new models.
First, not all datasets are suitable for comparing the classiﬁcation eﬀectiveness of the proposed methods since basic models can achieve very high accuracy on these datasets, like CWRU and XJTU-SY.

First, not all datasets are suitable for comparing the classiﬁcation eﬀectiveness of the proposed methods since basic models can achieve very high accuracy on these datasets, like CWRU and XJTU-SY.
Second, the frequency domain input can achieve the highest accuracy in all datasets, so researchers should ﬁrst try to use the frequency domain as the input.

Fourth, when the accuracy of datasets is not very high, data augmentation methods improve the performance of models, especially for the time domain input.
Thus, more eﬀective data augmentation methods need to be investigated.
Finally, in some cases, it may be more suitable for splitting the datasets according to time sequences (order split) since the random split may provide a virtually high accuracy.

AE consists of an encoder and a decoder, which tries to reconstruct the input from the output of an encoder, and the reconstruction error is used as a loss function. In detail, an encoder takes x as an input and transforms it into a hidden representaion h which can be formualted as:
h = φ(W · x + b) (1) φ(·) denotes the nonlinear activation function (in this paper, we use ReLU), and W and b represent the weight and bias required to learn, respectively. After that, a decoder generates the output x′ from the hidden representaion h, which can be formulated as:

7. Data Split One common practice of data split in intelligent diagnosis is the random split strategy, and the diagram of this strategy is shown in Fig. 7. From this diagram, we stress the preprocessing step without overlap due to the fact that if the sample preparation process exists any overlap, the evaluation of classiﬁcation algorithms may have test leakage (if users split the training set and the testing set from the beginning of the preprocessing step, then they can use any processing to simultaneously deal with the training and testing sets, as shown in Fig. 8).
The formal way is that the training set is further split into the training set and the validation set for the model selection.
Fig. 7 shows the condition of 4-fold cross-validation, and we often use the average accuracy of 4-fold cross-validation to represent the generalization accuracy, if there is no testing set. In this paper, for testing convenience and time saving, we only use 1-fold validation and use the last epoch accuracy to represent the testing accuracy (we also list the maximum accuracy in the whole epochs for comparisons). It is worth noting that some papers use the maximum accuracy of the validation set, and this strategy is also dangerous because the validation set is used to select the parameters accidentally.
For industrial data, they are rarely random and are always sequential (they might contain trends or other temporal correlation). Therefore, it is more appropriate to split data according to time sequences (order split). The diagram of data split strategy according to time sequences is shown in Fig. 9. From this diagram, it can be observed that we split the training and testing sets with the time phase instead of splitting the data randomly. In addition, Fig. 9 also shows the condition of 4-fold cross-validation with time. In the following study, we will compare the results of this strategy with the random split strategy.

9.4. Results of Models From the results, we can observe that models, especially ResNet18, can achieve the best accuracy in most of datasets including CWRU, JNU, PU, SEU, and XJTU-SY. However, for MFPT and UoC, models belonging to AE can perform better than other models. This phenomenon may be caused by the size of datasets and the overﬁtting problem. Results of Data Normalization It is hard to conclude which data normalization method is the best one, and from the results, we can observe that the accuracy of diﬀerent data normalization methods also depends on the used models and datasets. In general, Z-score normalization can make models achieve better accuracy.
9.6. Results of Data Augmentation We can conclude that when the accuracy of datasets is already high enough, data augmentation methods may slightly degrade the performance because models have already ﬁtted original datasets well. More augmentation methods may change the distribution of the original data and make the learning process harder. However, when the accuracy of datasets is not very high, data augmentation methods improve the performance of models, especially for the time domain input.
Therefore, researchers can design other various data augmentation methods for their speciﬁc inputs.
9.7. Results of Data Splitting When the datasets are easy to handle (CWRU and XJTU-SY), the results between random split and order split are quite similar. However, the accuracy of some datasets (PU and UoC) decreases sharply when using order split. What we should pay more attention to is that whether randomly splitting these datasets has the risk of test leakage. It may be more suitable for splitting the datasets according to time sequences to verify the performance.
According to the above discussion, we summarize the following conclusion coming from the evaluation results. First, not all datasets are suitable for comparing the classiﬁcation eﬀectiveness of the proposed methods since basic models can achieve very high accuracy on these datasets, like CWRU and XJTU-SY. Second, the frequency domain input can achieve the highest accuracy in all datasets, so researchers should ﬁrst try to use the frequency domain as the input. Third, it is not necessary for CNN models to get the best results in all cases, and we also should consider the overﬁtting problem.

In this experiment, we adopt ResNet18 as the experimental model and only use two kinds of input types (the time domain input and the frequency domain input).

10.4. Few-Shot Learning In intelligent diagnosis, the amount of data is far from big data because of the preciousness of fault data and the high cost of fault simulation experiments, especially for the key components. To manifest the inﬂuence of the sample number on the classiﬁcation accuracy, we use the PU bearing dataset to design a few-shot training pattern with six groups of diﬀerent sample numbers in each class.
Results of the time domain input and the frequency domain input are shown in Fig. 14. It is shown that with the decrease of the sample number, the accuracy decreases sharply. As shown in Fig. 14, for the time domain input, the Best-Max accuracy decreases from 91.46% to 20.39% as the sample number decreases from 100 to 1. Meanwhile, the Best-Max accuracy decreases from 97.73% to 29.67% as the sample number decreases from 100 to 1 with the frequency domain input.
Although the accuracy can be increased after using FFT, it is still too low to be accepted when the number of samples is extremely small. It is necessary to develop methods based on few-shot learning to cope with application scenarios with limited samples.
Many DL-based few-shot learning models have been proposed in recent years [112], most of these methods adopt a meta-learning paradigm by training networks with a large number of tasks, which means that the big data in other related ﬁelds is necessary for these methods. In the ﬁeld of fault diagnosis, there is no relevant data with such a big size available, so methods embedding with physical mechanisms are required to address this problem eﬀectively.

10.5. Model selection For intelligent diagnosis, designing a neural network is not the ﬁnal goal, and our task is to apply the model to real industrial applications while designing a neural network is only a small part of our task. However, to achieve a good 29

eﬀect, we have to spend considerable time and energy on designing the corresponding networks. Because building a neural network is an iterative process consisting of repeated trial and error, and the performance of models should be fed back to us to adjust models. The single trial and error cost multiplied by the number of trial and error can easily reach a huge cost. Besides, reducing this cost is also the partial purpose of this benchmark study which provides some guidelines to choose a baseline model.
Actually, there is another way called neural architecture search (NAS) [113] to avoid the huge cost of trial and error.
NAS can allow designing a neural network automatically through searching for a speciﬁc network based on a speciﬁc dataset. Limited search space of the network is ﬁrst constructed according to the physical prior. After that, a neural network matching a speciﬁc dataset is sampled from the search space through reinforcement learning, the evolutionary algorithm or the gradient strategy. Besides, the whole construction process does not require manual participation, which greatly reduces the cost of building a neural network and allows us to focus on speciﬁc engineering applications.
11. Conclusion In this paper, we collect nine publicly available datasets to evaluate the performance of MLP, AE, CNN, and RNN models. This work mainly focuses on evaluating DL-based intelligent diagnosis algorithms from diﬀerent perspectives and providing the benchmark accuracy (a lower bound) to avoid useless improvement. In addition, we release a code library for other researchers to test the performance of their own DL-based intelligent diagnosis models of these datasets.
We hope that the evaluation results and the code library could promote a better understanding of DL-based models and provide a uniﬁed framework for generating more eﬀective models. For further studies, we will focus on ﬁve listed issues (class imbalance, generalization ability, interpretability, few-shot learning, and model selection) to propose more customized works.

6 Introduction Generally, bearing inspection or housing inspection can identify  the cause of the problem. Often the cause is attributable to  poor lubrication, improper handling, selecting the wrong  bearing, or not enough study of the shaft and housing.  Usually the cause can be determined by considering  operation of the bearing before the failure, investigating  the lubrication conditions and the mounting condition,  and carefully observing the damaged bearing itself.
Sometimes bearings are damaged and fail both quickly and  unexpectedly. Such premature failure is different from fatigue  failure which is due to flaking. Bearing life can be separated  and categorized into two types: premature failure and normal  rolling contact fatigue.w When a rolling bearing is damaged during machine operation, the entire machine or  equipment may seize or malfunction. Since bearings that fail prematurely or unexpectedly  cause trouble, it is important to be able to identify and predict failure beforehand, if possible,  so that preventive measures can be adopted.

7 NEW BEARING DOCTOR Bearing Handling & Maintenance Precautions for Handling Since rolling bearings are high precision machine parts, they  must be handled carefully. Even if high quality bearings are  used, their expected life and performance cannot be  attained if they are used improperly. The main precautions  to be observed  are as follows:
(1) Keep the bearings and surroundings clean: Dust and  dirt, even if invisible to the naked eye, have harmful ef fects  on bearings. It is necessary to prevent the entry of dust and  dirt by keeping the bearings and their environment as clean  as possible.
(2) Handle with care: Heavy shocks during handling may  scratch or cause other damage to the bearing possibly  resulting in bearing failure. Strong impacts may cause  brinelling, breaking or cracking.
(3) Use proper tools:  Always use the proper tool when hand ling bearings and  avoid general purpose tools.
(4) Protect bearings from corrosion:  Since perspiration on the hands and various other  contaminants may cause corrosion, keep your hands  clean when handling bearings. Wear gloves if possible.

8 Mounting It is advisable to study the bearing mounting thoroughly since  the quality of the bearing mounting influences the bearing’s  running accuracy, life and performance. It is recommended  that the mounting method includes the following steps.
› Clean the bearing and surrounding parts.
› Check the dimensions and finish conditions of related parts.
› Follow mounting procedure.
› Check if the bearing is mounted correctly.
› Supply with correct kind and quantity of lubricant.
Since most bearings rotate with the shaft, the bearing  mounting method is generally an interference (tight) fit for  the inner ring and shaft while giving a clearance (loose) fit  for the outer ring and housing.
Check the Operation After mounting the bearing, it is important to carry out  an operating test to confirm that the bearing is mounted  properly. Table 1 indicates operating test methods.  If irregularities are detected, immediately suspend the test  and consult Table 2 which lists appropriate countermeasures  to specific bearing problems.
It is necessary to periodically inspect and maintain the  bearing and its operating conditions in order to maximise  the bearing life. In general, the following method is adopted.
(1) Inspection under operating conditions To determine the bearing replacement periods and  replenishment intervals for lubricant, investigate the  lubricant properties and consider factors such as  operating temperature, vibration, and bearing noise.  (Refer to Section »Performance Factors« for more details.) (2) Inspection of the bearing Be sure to investigate the bearing thoroughly during times  of periodic machine inspection and part replacement. Check  the raceway condition. Determine if damage exists. Confirm  if the bearing can be reused or should be replaced. (Refer to  Section »Bearing Inspection« for more details.) Bearing Handling & Maintenance

10 Bearing Performance Factors Bearing Noise During operation, sound detection instruments (stethoscope,  NSK Bearing Monitor, etc.) can be used to investigate the volume  and characteristics of the bearing rotation noise. It is possible  to distinguish bearing damage such as small flaking by means  of its unusual yet characteristic noise.
Bearing Vibration Bearing irregularities can be analyzed by measuring the  vibrations of an operating machine. A frequency spectrum  analyser is used to measure the magnitude of vibration and  the distribution of the frequencies. Test results enable the  determination of the likely cause of the bearing irregularity.  The measured data varies depending on the operating  conditions of the bearing and the location of the vibration  pick-up. Therefore, the method requires the determination  of evaluation standards for each measured machine.
It is useful to be able to detect irregularities from the  bearing vibration pattern during operation. Please refer  to the NSK pamphlet CAT. No. E410 (Bearing Monitor)  for more information about such a device.
Bearing Temperature Generally, the bearing temperature can be estimated from the  temperature of the housing outside surface, but a preferable  way is to obtain direct measurements from the bearing outer  ring by a probe going through an oil hole. Usually, the bearing  temperature gradually increases after the start of operation  until reaching a steady state condition about 1 or 2 hours  later. The bearing steady state temperature depends on load,  rotational speed and heat transfer properties of the machine.  Insufficient lubrication or improper mounting might cause the  bearing temperature to rise rapidly. In such a case, suspend the  machine operation and adopt an appropriate countermeasure.
Effects of Lubrication The two main purposes of lubrication are to minimise friction  and reduce wear inside bearings that might otherwise fail  prematurely. Lubrication provides the following advantages:
› Reduction of Friction and Wear  Direct metallic contact between the bearing rings, rolling  elements and cage, which are the basic components of  a bearing, is prevented by an oil film which reduces the  friction and wear in the contact areas.
› Extension of Fatigue Life  The rolling fatigue life of bearings depends greatly upon  the viscosity and film thickness between the rolling contact  surfaces. A heavy film thickness prolongs the fatigue life,  but it is shortened if the viscosity of the oil is too low so  that the film thickness is insufficient.
› Dissipation of Frictional Heat and Cooling  Circulation lubrication may be used to carry away either  frictional heat or heat transferred from the outside to prevent  the bearing from overheating and the oil from deteriorating.
› Sealing and Rust Prevention  Adequate lubrication also helps to prevent foreign  material from entering the bearings and guards against  corrosion or rusting.
Key bearing performance factors during operation are bearing noise, vibration, temperature,  and lubricant state. Please refer to Table 2 if any operation irregularities are detected.

11 NEW BEARING DOCTOR Selection of Lubrication Bearing lubrication methods are divided into two  main categories: grease lubrication and oil lubrication.  A lubrication method is adopted that matches the  application conditions and application purpose in  order to attain best performance from the bearing. › Grease lubrication  Grease is a lubricant that is made from base oil,  thickener, and additives. When selecting a grease,  it is necessary to select a grease that is suitable to  the bearing application conditions. There are large  differences in performance even between different  brands of the same type of grease. Therefore  special attention must be given to grease selection.  Table 5 (page 12) gives examples of applications  and grease consistency.

15 NEW BEARING DOCTOR When inspecting a bearing during periodic inspection of equipment, operating  inspections, or replacement of adjacent parts, determine the condition of the  bearing and if its continued service is advisable.
A record should be kept of the inspection and external  appearance of dismounted bearings. After taking a grease  sample and measuring the quantity of residual grease,  the bearing should be cleaned. Also, determine whether  abnormalities and damage exist in the cage, fitting surfaces,  rolling element surfaces and raceway surfaces. Refer to  page 16 regarding the observation of running traces on  the raceway surface.
When evaluating whether a bearing can be re-used or not,  the following points need to be considered: degree of  bearing damage, machine performance, critical nature of  the application, operating conditions, inspection interval. If  the inspection reveals bearing damage or abnormalities, then  try to confirm the cause and determine a countermeasure by  referring to page 18 and then carry out the countermeasure.
If your inspection discovers any of the following kinds of  damage, which would prevent the bearing from being  reused, then the bearing must be replaced with a new one.
(1) Cracks or chipping in the cage, rolling elements,  or raceway ring.
(2) Flaking in the rolling elements or raceway ring.
(3) Notable scoring on the rolling elements, rib face (collar),  or raceway surface.
(4) Notable wear on the cage or loose rivets.
(5) Flaws or rust on the rolling elements or raceway surface.
(6) Notable dents on the rolling elements or raceway surface.
(7) Notable creep of the outer ring outside surface  or inner ring bore.
(8) Discoloration due to heating.
(9) Serious damage on shield or seal of grease packed bearings.

If the running traces are clearly defined, it is possible to  determine whether the bearing is carrying a radial load,  axial load or moment load. Also, the roundness condition of  the bearing can be determined. Check whether unexpected  bearing loads or large mounting errors occurred. Also,  determine the probable cause of the bearing damage.
